name: Enamel reshaping / contouring

lead: Enamel reshaping smooths chips, evens out edges and slightly changes the length or shape of a tooth, mostly on the front teeth. People use it for quick, subtle fixes to teeth that are almost right already.

A dentist removes a thin layer of enamel using fine diamond burs, discs, strips or lasers, then polishes the surface. The change is visible straight away. It is described as a subtle change rather than a fix for major alignment problems, and no clinical studies specific to the procedure were found.

paras: It is usually a single-visit treatment, and since enamel has no nerve endings it often needs no anaesthetic. People often pair it with whitening or bonding, and it is a common small step in a smile makeover.
Enamel does not grow back, so the change is permanent. Taking off too much can expose dentin and cause temporary sensitivity.

angle.text: Enamel reshaping is used for quick, subtle fixes to uneven edges, chips and slightly long or pointed teeth, mostly on front teeth. A dentist shaves a thin layer of enamel and polishes it, and the change is visible straight away.

lead: Enamel reshaping, also called enamel contouring, enameloplasty or odontoplasty, is a cosmetic dental procedure in which a dentist removes a small amount of the outer surface of a tooth to change its shape, length or edge, or to smooth chips and minor irregularities [1]. It is typically applied to front teeth.

Descriptions of the procedure say it is quick, often completed in a single visit, and that enamel contains no nerve endings, so anaesthesia is frequently unnecessary [2]. Because enamel does not regenerate, the change is permanent, and removing too much can expose the underlying dentin [1][2].

No clinical studies specific to the procedure were located for this article; the available descriptions come from general encyclopedic sources on cosmetic dentistry, one of which notes that parts of its own material rest on dental-practice and consumer websites [2].
infobox: Cosmetic dentistry is not recognised as a specialty by the American Dental Association [1]

paras: The procedure removes small amounts of enamel to correct chips, alter tooth length or shape, address differences in tooth size or smooth the look of slightly crooked teeth [1]. One source describes it as fast and says it can in some cases be used instead of braces for minor irregularities [1]. A further source reports that amounts on the order of 0.3 to 0.5 mm are cited for subtle changes, using diamond burs, discs, strips or lasers, followed by polishing [2].
It is not described as suitable for significant misalignment, which orthodontic treatment addresses [2].

Sources agree that removed enamel cannot be replaced and that over-removal may expose dentin [1][2]. Temporary sensitivity to heat, cold or sweet foods is described as possible when enamel becomes thin [2]. Practitioners are described as favouring conservative, minimally invasive removal [2].

Enamel contouring is listed alongside whitening, bonding, veneers, bridges, implants and gum contouring as a standard cosmetic option [1]. It is often discussed as part of planned smile design, where tooth proportions and display are assessed together [2]. Cosmetic dentistry has been criticised in some quarters over informed consent, overtreatment and marketing, and the ADA does not approve the credentials of cosmetic-dentistry accreditation bodies [1][2].
